SOURCE: "LLM-as-a-Verifier: A General-Purpose Verification Framework". Jacky Kwok, Shulu Li, Pranav Atreya, Yuejiang Liu, Yixing Jiang, Chelsea Finn, Marco Pavone, Ion Stoica, Azalia Mirhoseini (Stanford University, UC Berkeley, NVIDIA Research). Preprint; the only venue marking is "arXiv:2607.05391v2 [cs.AI] 7 Jul 2026". The printed title is not "Verification as a Scaling Axis"; that phrase is only the paper's framing.

COVERAGE: 31 of 31 pages, 95,885 of 95,885 chars. Body is p1-16, references p17-25 (skimmed for origins), appendices A-B.7 on p26-31 (read in full). Figures 1, 5, 9 and 10 are plots whose values I took from captions and text only.

CLAIMS (ranked)

- claim: Taking the expectation over score-token logprobs, instead of the argmax token, removes ties and raises pairwise accuracy; one verifier pass matches a 16-pass discrete judge.
  number: verifier 74.7% (K=1) to 77.5% (K=16); judge 71.8 / 74.4 / 74.7% at K=1/4/16; judge tie rate 26.7% to 5.5%, verifier 0.0%
  setup: Terminal-Bench V2, Gemini 2.5 Flash as verifier, G=20, pairwise accuracy (correct trajectory scored above failed one for the same task, ties counted as half), "200 randomly sampled trajectories" across harnesses
  quote: "The judge produces ties in26.7% of comparisons at𝑘=1 due to coarse discrete scoring, decreasing to5.5% at 𝑘=16as averaging breaks ties. In contrast, the verifier yields zero ties."
  where: p9, Fig. 7

- claim: Accuracy rises along three axes: granularity, repetition, criteria decomposition.
  number: 73.1% to 77.5% (G=1 to 20, at K=16); 74.7% to 77.4% (K=1 to 16, at G=20); 75.2-76.4% for a single criterion against 78.3% for the ensemble of three (Specification, Output, Errors)
  setup: same as above
  quote: "rising from73.1% at 𝐺=1 to 77.5% at 𝐺=20, from74.7% at 𝐾=1 to 77.4% at 𝐾=16, and from75.2%–76.4% for any single criterion to78.3% when the three criteria are ensembled"
  where: p7 (Fig. 4 on p3)

- claim: In one case study, a discrete 1-5 judge ties almost every time, and the expectation over the same scale breaks every tie.
  number: judge 12 correct / 88 tie / 0 wrong; verifier G=5 69 / 0 / 31; verifier G=20 77 / 0 / 23, out of 100
  setup: one trajectory pair, `query-optimize` task, Opus 4.5 with OpenHands, Gemini 2.5 Flash scoring, 100 repeats
  quote: "The discrete1–5judge produces ties in88/100evaluations."
  where: p8, Table 2. Note that breaking ties also creates 23-31 wrong orderings where the judge had none.

- claim: Best-of-N selection with the verifier beats Pass@1 but leaves much of the oracle gap open.
  number: Terminal-Bench V2 83.1 to 86.5% (oracle 92.1%, N=5 GPT-5.5 with Capy); SWE-Bench Verified 76.1 to 78.2% (oracle 84.4%, N=3, one each from Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash, MiniMax M2.5, mini-swe-agent); MedAgentBench 70.2 to 73.3% (oracle 75.0%, N=5 Opus 4.8)
  setup: verifier Gemini 2.5 Flash, G=20, K=8, three criteria, pivot tournament
  quote: "Terminal-Bench V2 GPT-5.5 (84.7%) Opus 4.7 (80.2%) G3.1 Pro (80.2%) 83.1% 92.1%86.5%"
  where: p10, Table 3

- claim: The Probabilistic Pivot Tournament cuts pairwise comparisons from O(N²) to O(Nk) with little accuracy loss, and its ring pass puts each candidate once in slot A and once in slot B to cancel position bias.
  number: k=3: 66.17% at 4,723 pairs; k=9: 67.13% at 9,630; full round-robin 67.42% at 13,111; V1 best 65.85% at 7,000; pass@1 52.64%
  setup: Terminal-Bench V2, 89 tasks, N=20 trajectories per task, Terminus-2
  quote: "PPT𝑘=9(ours)9,63067.13 / Full Round-Robin13,111 67.42"
  where: p27-28, Table 9

- claim: Models without logprobs can be handled in two stages: the closed model writes reasoning, then an open model scores it via logits.
  number: K=1: 80.1% against 74.9% with a 10.9% tie rate; K=16: 81.2% against 79.1%
  setup: Terminal-Bench V2 pairs, GPT-5.5 reasoning then Gemini 2.5 Flash G=20, 400 bootstrap subsamples
  quote: "(80.1% vs. 74.9%) and eliminates the10.9% tie rate"
  where: p31, Table 12

- claim: On video, the zero-shot verifier beats trained reward models and the discrete judge.
  number: 87.4% against judge 70.8%, RoboReward-8B 81.4%, Robometer-4B 78.8%, TOPReward 74.7%; 81.5% at K=1
  setup: RoboRewardBench, 500 pairs, Qwen 3.6 35B, G=20, K=8
  quote: "LLM-as-a-Judge (Discrete) 70.8 LLM-as-a-Verifier (Ours) 87.4"
  where: p11, Table 4; p30

- claim: The verifier score tracks task progress.
  number: Spearman VOC 0.848±0.012 on successful and 0.769±0.016 on failed trajectories (code); 0.966 (robotics)
  setup: 500 Terminal-Bench V2 trajectories, Gemini 2.5 Flash, G=20; 500 RoboReward trajectories, Qwen 3.6, K=5
  quote: "Successful0.848±0.012 Failed0.769±0.016"
  where: p13, Tables 6-7

- claim: Used as a dense RL reward, it improves sample efficiency.
  number: about 1.8x on LIBERO (final success 0.76 against 0.69, n=5 seeds); about 1.1x on MATH (n=3)
  quote: "≈1.8× fewer environment steps and reaches a higher final success rate (0.76 vs. 0.69)"
  where: p14, Fig. 9

LIMITS
- Conceded (Appendix A, p26): needs scoring-token logits; criteria are hand-designed; the RL experiments are "limited to single-turn settings". Repetition gains diminish "due to correlated biases on harder examples" (p9).
- Not shown:
  - No cost, latency or token figures for G=20, K=8, C=3 with pairwise comparison.
  - The state-of-the-art claims compare best-of-3 or best-of-5 selection against single-run leaderboard entries, so compute is not matched.
  - No confidence intervals on the headline or scaling numbers. The gains are a few points on n=200, and the signal-to-noise ratio moves only 0.775 to 0.799.
  - "Calibrated" is asserted from that ratio, with no calibration measurement.
  - Position bias is said to cancel in the ring pass but is never measured.
  - No agreement with human raters, except a robotics mean absolute error of 1.11 to 0.72.
  - All scaling ablations use one verifier (Gemini 2.5 Flash) on one benchmark.
  - Self-preference bias is not tested.
- Dated: model names and leaderboard positions (GPT-5.5, Opus 4.7/4.8) are a mid-2026 snapshot.

BUILDS ON: Zheng et al. 2023 (MT-Bench, the judge baseline); Singh et al. 2026 (V1, pairwise self-verification, the ranking baseline); Liu et al. 2023 (G-Eval) and Fu et al. 2023 (GPTScore) for probability-based scoring; Liu et al. 2024 (HD-Eval) for criteria decomposition; the Bradley-Terry model (no citation given); Cobbe et al. 2021 and Lightman et al. 2023 for outcome and process reward models; Ma et al. 2025 for VOC; Brown et al. 2024 and Snell et al. 2024 for repeated sampling.

CODE (p5):
- Prompt tail: "<score_A> INTEGER_1_TO_20 </score_A> <score_B> INTEGER_1_TO_20 </score_B> Rating Rules: Rate correctness on a 1–20 scale based on evaluation criteria (1 = incorrect, 10 = borderline, 20 = correct)".
- Eq. 3.1: R(x,τ) = 1/(CK) Σ_c Σ_k Σ_g p_θ(v_g|x,c,τ) φ(v_g).
- Eq. 3.2 (p6): P(τi ≻ τj) = 1/(1+exp(−(R_i − R_j))).
- Pair count for the tournament (p7): N + k(N−k) + C(k,2).

FIGURES: Figure 7, p9, "Verifier (continuous) vs. Judge (discrete) on Terminal-Bench V2 across k∈{1,4,16}". It puts accuracy and tie rate side by side, which shows the cost of discrete scoring and that repetition only partly fixes it faster than prose can.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction is clean apart from dropped spaces in places and flattened equations and tables. No instructions aimed at the reader; the only instruction-like text is the paper's own verifier prompt.
- Internal inconsistencies in the source:
  - Accuracy at K=16 is printed as 77.4% on p7 and 77.5% on p3 and p9.
  - The prompt note says "letter-based scale instead of digits", but the template shows integers 1-20.
  - "G=1" granularity is never defined.
  - Oracle is 98.9% in Fig. 5 (pooled across the whole leaderboard) and 92.1% in Table 3 (N=5 pool). These are different pools.
  - Terminus-2 pass@1 is 52.64% in Table 9 but 62.9% and 68.5% in Table 8. Models and pools differ and the paper does not reconcile them.
  - The text cites "Eq. 1" where it means Eq. 3.1.
